structure.overview: Merck Canada Inc. sought judicial review of the Minister of Health's refusal to add Patent No 2,830,806 to the Patent Register due to late submission during the COVID-19 pandemic. Merck argued that the Time Limits Act suspended the 30-day deadline or that the Minister unreasonably refused to extend it, but the court found the Minister's decision reasonable and dismissed the application. The court held that the Time Limits Act did not suspend the deadline and that the Minister had no discretion to extend it under the PM(NOC) Regulations.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck seeks judicial review of the Minister's refusal to add Patent No 2,830,806 to the Patent Register due to late submission.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck argues the Time Limits Act suspended the 30-day deadline or the Minister unreasonably refused to extend it during COVID-19.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister's decision was reasonable and the judicial review application is dismissed.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Merck markets KEYTRUDA®, approved in Canada in 2015 for advanced-stage cancers.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: KEYTRUDA® is an innovative drug with market exclusivity until 2023 and a six-year no-file period until 2021.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: One patent, No 2,691,357, is listed for KEYTRUDA®, expiring in 2028.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The 806 Patent, issued in 2020, claims a formulation of KEYTRUDA®.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Merck USA discovered the 806 Patent issuance late and submitted patent lists after business hours, deemed filed next business day.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Subsection 4(6) of the PM(NOC) Regulations requires patent list submission within 30 days after patent issuance.

citations.cite: s 4(6) of the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, SOR/93-133
citations.why: Provides the 30-day patent list submission rule

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Minister preliminarily determined patent lists were late; Merck responded with representations and evidence.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Minister confirmed no discretion to extend 30-day deadline and Time Limits Act does not extend it.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck says refusal to list 806 Patent deprives protections and litigation advantages under PM(NOC) Regulations.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck argues listing 806 Patent causes no prejudice and refusal causes harm due to frozen register provision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Issues: Was Minister's determination on Time Limits Act and discretion to extend 30-day period reasonable?

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Minister's decision reviewed for reasonableness per Vavilov and Elanco standards.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 100
citations.why: Sets reasonableness standard for review

citations.cite: Elanco v Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FC 5 at para 50
citations.why: Supports reasonableness standard application

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Statutory interpretation by administrative decision makers must follow text, context, and purpose per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Vavilov at para 120
citations.why: Explains statutory interpretation principles

citations.cite: Canada Trustco Mortgage Co v Canada, 2005 SCC 54 at para 10
citations.why: Supports use of ordinary meaning when words are precise

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Decision makers must not choose inferior interpretations for expediency but discern legislative intent per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Vavilov at para 121
citations.why: Prohibits choosing inferior interpretations for expediency

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Time Limits Act s 6(1) suspends only court-related limitation periods and time limits during COVID-19.

citations.cite: Time Limits Act, SC 2020, c 11, s 6(1)
citations.why: Defines suspended time limits under the Act

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Time Limits Act s 6(1) applies only to court proceedings and related time limits.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck argues s 4(6) is a gateway to litigation provisions under s 6(1) of PM(NOC) Regulations.

citations.cite: s 6(1) of the PM(NOC) Regulations
citations.why: Merck relies on litigation provision timing

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck compares 30-day listing period to notice requirement in Bannon, a limitation within a limitation.

citations.cite: Bannon v Thunder Bay (City), 2000 CarswellOnt 1307 (ONCA)
citations.why: Merck relies on Bannon for limitation period analogy

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Bannon held notice requirement akin to limitation period, combined with actual limitation period.

citations.cite: Bannon at paras 22-23
citations.why: Explains Bannon's holding on notice as limitation

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck says patent listing is first step triggering 45-day limitation to commence court proceeding under PM(NOC).

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Bannon found notice promotes diligence and timely investigation, similar to limitation periods.

citations.cite: Bannon at para 22
citations.why: Describes policy reasons for notice requirement

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds patent listing differs from limitation periods; it is remote from court proceedings and lacks precipitating event.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court disagrees that PM(NOC) Regulations focus solely on litigation initiation; listing has broader advantages.

citations.cite: GD Searle & Co v Canada (Health), 2009 FCA 35 at para 13
citations.why: Court disagrees with Merck's litigation-centred view

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 5(1) requires second person to comply with patent owner consent, acceptance, or serve NOA before litigation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Dispute and parties arise only after second person files submission and serves NOA, triggering litigation rights.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Listing patent is too remote from court proceeding to be a limitation period under Time Limits Act s 6(1).

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck stresses Time Limits Act's purpose to flexibly suspend or extend time limits during COVID-19.

citations.cite: Time Limits Act s 5(1)
citations.why: Merck cites Act's flexible suspension and extension purpose

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 5's 'in a flexible manner' refers to ministerial discretion under s 7, not to suspension of court proceeding time limits under s 6.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The ViiV decision about suspension of s 6(1) time periods does not apply to the 30-day period in s 4(6), which was never suspended.

citations.cite: ViiV Healthcare et al v Sandoz Canada Inc, 2020 FC 1040
citations.why: ViiV's suspension ruling does not affect s 4(6) deadline here

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: ViiV contradicts the Minister's view on Time Limits Act's effect, but the Minister's finding on s 4(6) deadline remains sound.
idea_list: Minister's determination on s 4(6) remains sound

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck argues the Minister had discretion to list the 806 Patent and unreasonably declined to exercise it, citing jurisprudence and 2017 amendments.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck relies on Procter & Gamble case where the Minister added a late patent to the Patent Register despite late submission.

citations.cite: Procter & Gamble Pharmaceuticals Canada, Inc v Canada (Minister of Health), 2003 FCT 583
citations.why: Merck cites it to support Minister's discretion to add late patent

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Justice Gauthier dismissed a motion to strike the late patent listing due to a clerical error, finding it not plainly ineligible.

citations.cite: Procter & Gamble Pharmaceuticals Canada, Inc v Canada (Minister of Health), 2003 FCT 583
citations.why: Reports Justice Gauthier's decision on patent eligibility

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: An appeal dismissed the challenge to the patent listing on estoppel grounds due to failure to challenge earlier.

citations.cite: Procter & Gamble Pharmaceuticals Canada, Inc v Canada (Minister of Health), 2003 FCA 467
citations.why: Reports appellate dismissal on estoppel grounds

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Procter & Gamble decisions provide weak authority for Minister's discretion to add late patents, as the patent was added within 30 days.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: PM(NOC) Regulations timelines are strict; Hoffman-La Roche held no discretion to accept late filings without clear statutory authority.

citations.cite: Hoffman-La Roche Ltd v Canada (Health), 2005 FC 1415
citations.why: Supports strict interpretation of PM(NOC) timelines and no discretion for late filings

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Previous cases affirm strict timing for patent listing to protect patentees and ensure affordable medicines; ViiV confirms stringent timelines.

citations.cite: Fournier Pharma Inc v Canada (Attorney General), [1999] 1 FC 327
citations.why: Supports necessity of strict timelines

citations.cite: Immunex Corporation v Canada (Health), 2008 FC 1409
citations.why: Confirms strict timing deadlines

citations.cite: ViiV Healthcare et al v Sandoz Canada Inc, 2020 FC 1040
citations.why: Confirms PM(NOC) Regulations involve stringent timelines

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Merck argues 2017 amendments expanded Minister's discretionary powers to add or refuse patent lists under ss 3(2) to 3(2.3).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The 2017 amendments did not change patent listing eligibility or confer new discretion; Regulatory Impact Statement confirms unchanged criteria.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister's decision was reasonable, justified, intelligible, and transparent; judicial review application is dismissed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court commends counsel for the quality of their written and oral submissions.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: By agreement, no costs are awarded to either party.
